method:
One half is technical:
Coding—deciding, for instance, whether to use a sprite sheet or CSS transforms.
Color palettes and aesthetics.
How content displays across different screen sizes.
How to organize HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
Integrating an LLM (e.g., how to implement an "AI" button).
The other half is about meaning:
The quality of your research—what facts have you uncovered about the object?
Does it tell a story? Does it invite the audience to see the object in an entirely new light? Simply stacking facts is less effective than immersing the viewer in an experience (for example, pairing a flashlight with a mining theme—technology isn't just a collection of parts; it’s something used within a specific context).
Be prepared to explain what you researched, what you read, and how specific research findings informed your design decisions.

Thursday's class
1. Statements of meaning
2. Artist as questioner
3. Neutral questions
4. Opinions
related_work:
1. Statements of meaning: Respondents share what they find interesting, moving, or striking about the work. Focus only on the effective elements; do not mention what you dislike.
2. Artist as questioner: The artist specifies the type of feedback they are looking for—for example, "I was aiming for a blend of pixel art and hand-drawn styles; does that come across?" Respondents should address only this specific question, without veering off into other topics.
3. Neutral questions: Respondents reframe "I don't like X" into "Why did you choose X?" For instance: "Why did you choose to include glasses?" or "What was the biggest challenge you faced during the process?"
4. Opinions: The facilitator asks the artist, "Would you like to hear some opinions?" The artist may decline. If they agree, respondents should preface their remarks with "In my view..."—remember that opinions are not facts. Instead of saying "It’s not original," one might say, "To me, it looks a bit like a template."
After these four steps, you can move on to other discussions, such as potential next steps or the subject matter itself. Feel free to use a mix of Chinese and English; the most important thing is that your feedback is clearly understood.
conclusion_future_work:
CSS transform: Programmatic—you specify the movement (e.g., "move right by 20, up by 10") and the duration, and CSS handles the interpolation. The drawback: you can only animate an entire element as a single unit.
Sprite sheet + `steps()`: You take an animation created in external software—such as rendered frames from Blender, a sequence of uniform-sized frames from Photoshop, or a composite image assembled via ImageMagick—and play them back frame by frame. This approach is ideal for organic motion or scenarios where multiple layers move simultaneously (e.g., a frog’s chest rising and falling, or grass swaying).
Why not just use video? Web animations are interactive—they can be triggered by clicks or scrolling, or even respond dynamically to the speed of a user's scroll. Furthermore, sprite sheets are lightweight, compatible with all browsers, and require no additional software to run.
Later on, you will explore techniques like Blender skeletal rigging, frame-by-frame hand-drawn animation using Grease Pencil, and the use of layered, deconstructible elements that can fly apart. For now, restricting you to sprite sheets or CSS transforms is a deliberate challenge—it forces you to transform static objects into dynamic, interactive experiences.

Thursday’s Class
I completed my "Project 0," highlighting key elements through fixed animated interactions and an introduction to local AI. I also sought feedback on how well my objects were received; meanwhile, I noticed that some of my classmates had developed more comprehensive interaction methods—an approach I can certainly learn from and incorporate into my own work.
results_discussion:
Don’t let your face betray your true thoughts: You might say, "The structure is good," but if your expression screams, "This is terrible," the other person will see right through it. The goal isn’t to learn how to hide your emotions, but rather to shift your focus toward the elements that are actually working.
Make feedback specific and actionable: Saying "I don’t like it" is useless. Instead, try something like, "The color scheme makes it look like a video game rather than something from the real world." This is helpful to Boyd, because his original intent was "cute yet realistic"—but the current result feels "game-like."
Don’t offer critiques on things no one asked about (e.g., "I don’t like your shoes"—when nobody asked for your opinion).
If you call something "cute," be prepared to elaborate: In class, Han Yi described Boyd’s glasses as "cute." When Boyd asked, "What makes them cute?" Han Yi replied, "The style and the color—the blue." Boyd responded, "Exactly—just point out what’s working."
Follow up your feedback by explaining the impact on you as a viewer: For instance, if you say something "looks like a template," add, "It makes me less curious to learn more."
title: Project 0 crit/A Trip to Bristol
introduction:
A "crit" (critique) consists of presenting your work and receiving constructive feedback. The term "critical" here does not imply something negative; rather, it is about examining the creator’s intentions and the extent to which those intentions were realized.
On Thursday, everyone has two responsibilities: 
① to present their own work and receive feedback, and 
② to provide meaningful feedback to others (Boyd suggests the latter might even be more important).
Boyd is explicit: everyone must provide feedback to every person who presents. Whether you find a piece boring, confusing, or even dislike it—that’s all fine—but silence is not an option. "Better to say something wrong than to say nothing at all."
Perfection is not required: "I showed you one of my own terrible pieces; that sets the baseline—just aim to be somewhere near that level."

On Thursday, we presented our respective websites. It went a bit more smoothly than I had anticipated; everyone took turns introducing their own sites and the content within them. My own project was a website about universal chargers, and I did my best to explain its content. During the session, Boyd also asked us to provide feedback on our classmates' work, so I offered my own suggestions as best I could.

On Friday, I went to Bristol with my classmates.I experienced a unique repair culture in Bristol. I met many people involved in the "repair culture." In the first project, I explored the concept of a "cultural twin" and experienced a unique 3D spatial culture—it was truly fascinating. In the second project, I looked into the repurposing of electronic waste. By taking various items apart, I discovered that much of what is discarded as e-waste actually contains components with the potential for reuse.Afterward, I went with my classmates to check out the night scenery in Bristol, had a meal at a Chinese restaurant, and got a taste of the nightlife. I headed back the next morning.
